notes.overview: This chapter covers the basic life processes that maintain the body of an organism, namely nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion, comparing how different organisms - from single-celled amoeba to complex plants and humans - carry out each function.

sections.title: 1. Nutrition: Autotrophic and Heterotrophic
sections.content: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and utilise food for energy, growth and repair. Autotrophic nutrition is the mode in which organisms (green plants and some bacteria) synthesise their own food from simple inorganic materials like carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight and chlorophyll, through the process of photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> (sunlight, chlorophyll) -> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Heterotrophic nutrition is the mode in which organisms cannot make their own food and depend on other organisms, and is further classified as saprophytic (feeding on dead/decaying matter, e.g. fungi), parasitic (deriving nutrition from a host, e.g. Cuscuta) or holozoic (ingesting solid food, e.g. most animals).

sections.title: 2. Photosynthesis: Site and Steps
sections.content: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in the leaves within chloroplasts, which contain the pigment chlorophyll that absorbs light energy; the process involves three main events - absorption of light energy by chlorophyll, conversion of light energy to chemical energy and splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen, and finally the reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates. Stomata are tiny pores, mostly on the underside of leaves, that allow gaseous exchange (CO2 in, O2 out) and are regulated by guard cells that swell or shrink to open or close the pore.

sections.title: 3. Human Digestive System
sections.content: Human digestion begins in the mouth, where saliva (containing the enzyme salivary amylase) breaks down starch into sugars; food then travels via the oesophagus (through peristaltic movement) to the stomach, where gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid (to kill germs and provide an acidic medium) and the enzyme pepsin (which digests proteins). In the small intestine, bile (from the liver, stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fats into smaller globules, while pancreatic juice (from the pancreas) contains enzymes (trypsin for proteins, lipase for fats, amylase for starch) that complete digestion; the digested food is absorbed through finger-like projections called villi, and undigested waste passes to the large intestine, where water is absorbed before egestion through the anus.

sections.title: 4. Respiration
sections.content: Respiration is the process of breaking down food (glucose) to release energy for cellular activities, and can be aerobic (in the presence of oxygen, releasing more energy: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy) or anaerobic (in the absence of oxygen, releasing less energy, as in yeast producing ethanol and CO2, or in human muscle cells producing lactic acid during vigorous exercise causing cramps). In humans, air enters through the nostrils, passes through the trachea into the lungs, where it reaches millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli that provide a large surface area for the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide with blood capillaries.

sections.title: 5. Transportation in Human Beings
sections.content: The human circulatory system consists of the heart, blood vessels and blood; the heart is a four-chambered muscular organ (two atria and two ventricles) that pumps blood - the right side handles deoxygenated blood (from the body to the lungs) and the left side handles oxygenated blood (from the lungs to the body), and this separation prevents the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, which is important for the efficient double circulation needed by warm-blooded animals. Arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick, elastic walls, no valves, mostly oxygenated blood except the pulmonary artery), veins carry blood towards the heart (thinner walls, have valves to prevent backflow, mostly deoxygenated blood except the pulmonary vein), and capillaries are thin-walled vessels that allow exchange of materials between blood and tissues.

sections.title: 6. Transportation in Plants
sections.content: Plants transport water and minerals through xylem tissue via a unidirectional upward flow, driven mainly by transpiration pull (the evaporation of water from leaf surfaces through stomata creates suction that pulls water up from the roots) along with root pressure. Food (prepared by photosynthesis) is transported through phloem tissue, in both upward and downward directions, using energy from ATP, in a process called translocation, which moves sugars from the leaves (source) to storage organs and growing parts of the plant (sink).

sections.title: 7. Excretion
sections.content: Excretion is the biological process of removing harmful metabolic waste products from the body. In humans, the excretory system consists of a pair of bean-shaped kidneys, which contain millions of filtration units called nephrons that filter nitrogenous wastes (like urea) from the blood to form urine; urine passes from the kidneys through the ureters to the urinary bladder, where it is stored until it is released through the urethra. Plants excrete waste in different ways - excess water is removed by transpiration, other wastes are stored in leaves that later fall off (as in autumn), stored in cellular vacuoles, or excreted into the surrounding soil as resins and gums.

key_terms.Photosynthesis: The process by which green plants make their own food using carbon dioxide, water and sunlight, releasing oxygen.
key_terms.Peristalsis: The rhythmic, wave-like muscular contractions that move food along the alimentary canal.
key_terms.Alveoli: Tiny air sacs in the lungs that provide a large surface area for exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
key_terms.Nephron: The basic structural and functional filtration unit of the kidney.
key_terms.Translocation: The transport of food (sugars) prepared in the leaves to other parts of the plant through phloem.

important_facts: Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O -(sunlight, chlorophyll)-> C6H12O6 + 6O2
Aerobic respiration releases more energy than anaerobic respiration.
The human heart has four chambers: two atria (upper) and two ventricles (lower).
Xylem transports water and minerals (upward only); phloem transports food (both directions).
Kidneys filter blood to remove nitrogenous waste (urea) and form urine.

questions.question: Write the overall equation for photosynthesis and name the raw materials required.

rubric.point: Correct equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 (in sunlight, chlorophyll)
Raw materials: carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and chlorophyll

questions.model_answer: The overall equation for photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, yields C6H12O6 + 6O2. The raw materials required are carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and chlorophyll.

questions.question: What is the role of bile in digestion?

rubric.point: Bile emulsifies fats, breaking them into smaller globules
This increases the surface area for enzymes (lipase) to act, and bile is produced in the liver, stored in the gall bladder

questions.model_answer: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, emulsifies large fat globules into smaller droplets. This increases the surface area for pancreatic enzymes like lipase to break down fats more efficiently.

questions.question: Differentiate between arteries, veins and capillaries.

rubric.point: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, have thick elastic walls, no valves
Veins carry blood towards the heart, have thinner walls, have valves to prevent backflow
Capillaries are thin-walled vessels that allow exchange of materials between blood and tissues

questions.model_answer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, have thick and elastic walls to withstand high pressure, and lack valves. Veins carry blood back towards the heart, have thinner walls, and contain valves that prevent the backflow of blood. Capillaries are extremely thin-walled vessels connecting arteries and veins, allowing the exchange of nutrients, gases and wastes between the blood and body tissues.

questions.question: Describe the function of the kidney, ureter, urinary bladder and urethra in the human excretory system.

rubric.point: Kidneys filter blood and remove nitrogenous waste (urea) to form urine
Ureters carry urine from kidneys to the urinary bladder
Urinary bladder stores urine; urethra releases it out of the body

questions.model_answer: The kidneys filter nitrogenous wastes such as urea from the blood and form urine. Urine passes from each kidney through a ureter into the urinary bladder, where it is temporarily stored. When the bladder is full, urine is released to the outside through the urethra.

questions.question: Describe the pathway of air during breathing in humans and explain how oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged in the lungs. Also explain why the human heart is called a double circulatory pump.

rubric.point: Air path: nostrils -> trachea -> bronchi -> bronchioles -> alveoli
Alveoli provide a large surface area with thin walls and capillary network for gas exchange
Oxygen diffuses into blood, carbon dioxide diffuses out, at the alveoli
Double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle (once for pulmonary, once for systemic circuit)
This keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate, allowing more efficient oxygen supply to the body

questions.model_answer: During breathing, air enters through the nostrils, passes through the trachea, then into the bronchi and smaller bronchioles, finally reaching millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli in the lungs. The alveoli have thin walls and are surrounded by a dense network of blood capillaries, providing a large surface area for gas exchange - oxygen diffuses from the alveoli into the blood, while carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be exhaled. The human heart is called a double circulatory pump because blood passes through the heart twice during one complete circuit of the body: once through the pulmonary circulation (heart to lungs and back) to get oxygenated, and once through the systemic circulation (heart to body and back) to deliver oxygen to tissues. This four-chambered double circulation keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate, allowing more efficient supply of oxygen to the body, which is especially important for warm-blooded animals like humans.

questions.explanation: Cuscuta is a parasitic plant that derives nutrition directly from its host.

questions.explanation: Salivary amylase breaks down starch into simpler sugars in the mouth.

questions.question: Which enzyme present in pancreatic juice digests proteins in the small intestine?

questions.question: Finger-like projections in the small intestine that increase surface area for absorption of digested food are called:

questions.question: The tiny air sacs in the lungs where exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide takes place are called:
questions.explanation: Alveoli provide a large surface area with a rich capillary network for gas exchange.

questions.question: During anaerobic respiration, yeast breaks down glucose to produce:
questions.explanation: Yeast carries out anaerobic respiration (fermentation), producing ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.question: The upper two chambers of the human heart that receive blood are called the:
questions.explanation: The two atria are the upper chambers of the heart that receive incoming blood.

questions.question: Which blood vessel is an exception in that it carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, unlike other arteries.

questions.question: The transport of prepared food from the leaves to other parts of a plant through phloem is called:
questions.explanation: Translocation is the movement of food (sugars) through phloem, using energy from ATP.

questions.question: Plants get rid of excess water mainly through the process of:
questions.explanation: Excess water in plants is removed through transpiration from the leaf surface via stomata.

questions.question: Differentiate between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition, giving one example of each.

rubric.point: Autotrophic organisms synthesise their own food from CO2 and water using sunlight/chlorophyll, e.g. green plants
Heterotrophic organisms depend on other organisms for food, e.g. fungi/animals

questions.model_answer: Autotrophic nutrition is the mode in which organisms, such as green plants, synthesise their own food from simple inorganic substances like carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll. Heterotrophic nutrition is the mode in which organisms, such as fungi and animals, cannot make their own food and depend directly or indirectly on other organisms for nutrition.

questions.question: What are stomata and how do guard cells regulate their opening and closing?

rubric.point: Stomata are tiny pores mostly on the underside of leaves that allow gaseous exchange (CO2 in, O2 out) and water loss
Guard cells swell (pore opens) or shrink (pore closes) to regulate the size of the stomatal pore

questions.model_answer: Stomata are tiny pores, mostly present on the underside of leaves, that allow the exchange of gases (carbon dioxide in, oxygen out) needed for photosynthesis, as well as loss of water vapour. Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells, which swell with water to open the pore and shrink to close it, thereby regulating gaseous exchange and water loss.

questions.question: Explain the roles of hydrochloric acid and pepsin in the human stomach.

rubric.point: HCl kills germs/bacteria present in food and provides the acidic medium needed for pepsin to act
Pepsin is a protein-digesting enzyme that breaks down proteins in the acidic environment of the stomach

questions.model_answer: Hydrochloric acid, secreted by the gastric glands in the stomach wall, kills any germs present in food and creates the acidic medium required for the enzyme pepsin to work. Pepsin then acts on proteins present in food, breaking them down into simpler substances.

questions.question: Why is aerobic respiration considered more efficient (energy-releasing) than anaerobic respiration?

rubric.point: Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose in the presence of oxygen into CO2 and water
This releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration, which only partially breaks down glucose in the absence of oxygen

questions.model_answer: Aerobic respiration occurs in the presence of oxygen and completely breaks down glucose into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy. Anaerobic respiration occurs in the absence of oxygen and only partially breaks down glucose (into products like lactic acid or ethanol and CO2), releasing much less energy, making aerobic respiration far more efficient.

questions.question: What is transpiration pull, and how does it help in the transport of water in plants?

rubric.point: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from the leaf surface through stomata
This evaporation creates a suction/pulling force that draws water upward from the roots through the xylem

questions.model_answer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the surface of leaves through the stomata. As water evaporates from the leaf cells, it creates a suction force, called transpiration pull, that draws water (along with dissolved minerals) upward from the roots through the xylem to replace the water lost, enabling continuous upward water transport in plants.

questions.question: Trace the pathway of food from the mouth to the small intestine, mentioning the enzymes/secretions involved at each step.

rubric.point: Mouth: salivary amylase in saliva breaks down starch into sugars
Stomach: gastric glands secrete HCl and pepsin; HCl kills germs and provides acidic medium, pepsin digests proteins
Small intestine: bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice (trypsin, lipase, amylase) completes digestion of proteins, fats and starch

questions.model_answer: Digestion begins in the mouth, where saliva containing salivary amylase breaks down starch into simpler sugars. Food then passes through the oesophagus into the stomach, where gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid, which kills germs and provides an acidic medium, and pepsin, which digests proteins. In the small intestine, bile from the liver emulsifies fats into smaller globules, while pancreatic juice supplies trypsin (digests proteins), lipase (digests fats) and amylase (digests starch), completing the digestion process before absorption through the villi.

questions.question: Distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic respiration on the basis of oxygen requirement, end products and energy released.

rubric.point: Aerobic respiration occurs in the presence of oxygen; anaerobic occurs in its absence
Aerobic end products are CO2 and water; anaerobic end products are ethanol+CO2 (yeast) or lactic acid (muscles)
Aerobic respiration releases much more energy than anaerobic respiration

questions.model_answer: Aerobic respiration takes place in the presence of oxygen and completely breaks down glucose into carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy. Anaerobic respiration takes place in the absence of oxygen and only partially breaks down glucose, forming ethanol and carbon dioxide (as in yeast) or lactic acid (as in human muscle cells during vigorous exercise), and releases much less energy compared to aerobic respiration.

questions.question: Describe the process of photosynthesis, mentioning the site, raw materials and the main steps involved.

rubric.point: Occurs mainly in leaves, within chloroplasts containing chlorophyll
Raw materials: carbon dioxide (from air via stomata) and water (from roots via xylem)
Steps: absorption of light energy, conversion to chemical energy and splitting of water, reduction of CO2 to carbohydrates

questions.model_answer: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in the leaves, within chloroplasts that contain the pigment chlorophyll. The raw materials required are carbon dioxide, which enters through the stomata, and water, absorbed by the roots and transported via the xylem. The process involves three main steps: absorption of light energy by chlorophyll, conversion of this light energy into chemical energy along with splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen, and finally the reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates using the hydrogen obtained.

questions.question: How do plants get rid of their waste products? Describe three different methods.

rubric.point: Excess water is removed by transpiration through stomata
Some wastes are stored in leaves, which are later shed (e.g. in autumn)
Other wastes are stored in cellular vacuoles or excreted into the surrounding soil as resins and gums

questions.model_answer: Unlike animals, plants excrete waste in several ways. Excess water is removed through transpiration from the leaf surface via stomata. Some waste products are stored in leaves, which are later shed, as seen in autumn. Other waste substances are stored in cellular vacuoles, and some, such as resins and gums, are excreted into the surrounding soil, especially in old xylem tissue.

questions.question: Differentiate between the transport of materials through xylem and phloem in plants.

rubric.point: Xylem transports water and minerals; phloem transports food (sugars) prepared by photosynthesis
Movement in xylem is unidirectional (upward only); movement in phloem (translocation) can be in both directions
Xylem transport is driven mainly by transpiration pull; phloem transport uses energy from ATP

questions.model_answer: Xylem tissue transports water and minerals from the roots to the rest of the plant in one direction only (upward), driven mainly by transpiration pull along with root pressure. Phloem tissue transports food prepared by photosynthesis in the leaves to other parts of the plant, in both upward and downward directions, in a process called translocation, which requires energy supplied by ATP, unlike the largely passive movement of water in xylem.

questions.question: Describe the structure and function of the human digestive system, explaining the role of each major organ from the mouth to the large intestine.

rubric.point: Mouth: teeth and tongue mix food with saliva; salivary amylase begins starch digestion
Oesophagus carries food to the stomach by peristalsis; stomach secretes HCl and pepsin to digest proteins
Liver produces bile (stored in gall bladder) which emulsifies fats; pancreas secretes pancreatic juice with trypsin, lipase, amylase
Small intestine completes digestion and absorbs digested food through villi
Large intestine absorbs water from undigested waste, which is egested through the anus

questions.model_answer: Digestion begins in the mouth, where teeth break food into smaller pieces and saliva, containing salivary amylase, begins the digestion of starch. The food (bolus) then moves down the oesophagus to the stomach by peristaltic movement. In the stomach, gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid, which kills germs and provides an acidic medium, and pepsin, which digests proteins. The partially digested food then enters the small intestine, where bile (produced by the liver and stored in the gall bladder) emulsifies fats into smaller globules, and pancreatic juice from the pancreas supplies trypsin (digests proteins), lipase (digests fats) and amylase (digests starch) to complete digestion. The digested food is absorbed into the blood through finger-like projections called villi that line the small intestine. The undigested waste then passes into the large intestine, where water is absorbed, and the remaining solid waste is egested through the anus.

questions.question: Explain the different modes of nutrition found in living organisms, and describe in detail how green plants prepare their food through photosynthesis.

rubric.point: Autotrophic nutrition: organisms make their own food from CO2, water, sunlight and chlorophyll
Heterotrophic nutrition and its types: saprophytic, parasitic, holozoic, with examples
Photosynthesis site: chloroplasts in leaf cells containing chlorophyll
Steps of photosynthesis: absorption of light, splitting of water, reduction of CO2 to carbohydrates
Role of stomata and guard cells in gaseous exchange for photosynthesis

questions.model_answer: Organisms show two main modes of nutrition. Autotrophic nutrition is seen in green plants and some bacteria, which synthesise their own food from simple inorganic substances like carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight and chlorophyll. Heterotrophic nutrition is seen in organisms that cannot make their own food and depend on others; this is further divided into saprophytic nutrition (feeding on dead and decaying matter, e.g. fungi), parasitic nutrition (deriving nutrition from a living host without killing it, e.g. Cuscuta) and holozoic nutrition (ingesting solid food, e.g. most animals). Green plants prepare food through photosynthesis, which occurs mainly in the leaves, within chloroplasts containing the pigment chlorophyll. The process involves absorption of light energy by chlorophyll, conversion of this light energy into chemical energy with splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen, and finally the reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates. Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves the leaf through stomata, tiny pores whose opening and closing is regulated by guard cells that swell or shrink.

questions.topic: Case study - dialysis and the excretory system
questions.passage: A patient whose kidneys have failed is treated using a dialysis machine. The machine contains a dialysing fluid that matches blood's composition, except that it has no urea or other nitrogenous wastes in it. The patient's blood is passed through the machine and allowed to exchange substances with the dialysing fluid across a selectively permeable membrane before being returned to the body.

subquestions.question: Which organ's function is being artificially performed by the dialysis machine?
subquestions.explanation: Dialysis machines perform the blood-filtering function normally carried out by the kidneys.

subquestions.question: Why does urea move from the patient's blood into the dialysing fluid across the membrane?
options: Because urea is actively pumped out by the membrane using energy
Because the dialysing fluid has no urea, so urea diffuses down its concentration gradient
Because urea is chemically attracted to the membrane material
Because the membrane is impermeable to urea
subquestions.explanation: Since the dialysing fluid contains no urea, urea naturally diffuses from the (higher-concentration) blood into the (lower-concentration) fluid across the membrane - no energy is required.

subquestions.question: Name the basic filtration unit of the kidney, and briefly explain its role in forming urine.

rubric.point: The basic filtration unit of the kidney is the nephron
Each nephron filters blood (at the glomerulus/Bowman's capsule) and then selectively reabsorbs useful substances back into the blood, leaving wastes like urea to be excreted as urine

subquestions.model_answer: The basic filtration unit of the kidney is the nephron. Each nephron filters blood at the glomerulus (inside Bowman's capsule), and the filtrate then passes along the nephron's tubule, where useful substances (glucose, most water and salts) are selectively reabsorbed back into the blood, while wastes such as urea remain to be excreted as urine.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Kidneys help maintain the balance of water and salts in the body, in addition to removing nitrogenous waste.
Reason (R): The nephron, the functional unit of the kidney, filters blood and selectively reabsorbs water, salts and other useful substances back into the blood.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R explains the mechanism (selective reabsorption in the nephron) that lets the kidney regulate water/salt balance, not just remove waste.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Plants excrete nitrogenous waste the same way animals do, using a dedicated excretory organ.
Reason (R): Plants can get rid of excess water through transpiration, and store some waste products in leaves (which eventually fall off) or in cell vacuoles.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Plants do NOT have a dedicated excretory organ like animals' kidneys - so A is false. R correctly describes the very different, passive ways plants deal with waste (transpiration, storage in leaves/vacuoles).

questions.topic: Osmosis and water uptake in plant roots
questions.question: Which of the following statements is TRUE about the uptake of water in plants?
options: It occurs all the time due to diffusion
Water enters the roots due to osmosis
At night, when transpiration is low, roots do not take up water
The movement of water from roots to leaves is bidirectional
questions.explanation: Water enters root hair cells from the soil by osmosis (movement of water from a region of higher water concentration in the soil to lower water concentration inside the root hair cell, across the partially permeable cell membrane).

questions.topic: Oxygen saturation of haemoglobin with altitude
questions.question: Oxygen saturation refers to the extent to which haemoglobin is bound to oxygen. As altitude increases, atmospheric pressure (and hence available oxygen) decreases. Which trend correctly describes how oxygen saturation of haemoglobin changes as altitude increases?
options: It stays constant regardless of altitude
It rises sharply then falls sharply
questions.explanation: As altitude increases, atmospheric (and hence partial) oxygen pressure falls, so less oxygen is available to bind haemoglobin - oxygen saturation of haemoglobin therefore decreases with increasing altitude, which is why mountaineers at high altitude can experience oxygen deprivation.

questions.question: Patient X has a pancreatic condition in which the pancreas is not functioning adequately. Which dietary advice is a doctor likely to give?
options: Include a large amount of protein in the diet
Eat a diet with low fat content
questions.explanation: The pancreas secretes pancreatic lipase, essential for digesting fats; if the pancreas isn't functioning well, fat digestion is impaired, so a low-fat diet reduces the digestive burden the patient's body can't properly handle.

questions.topic: Role of hydrochloric acid in gastric digestion
questions.question: Gastric juice, secreted by gastric glands, contains hydrochloric acid, mucus and pepsin. Which activity will be affected in the absence of hydrochloric acid?
questions.explanation: Hydrochloric acid provides the acidic medium needed to activate pepsinogen into active pepsin, the enzyme that digests proteins - without HCl, protein digestion in the stomach is impaired.

questions.question: The lining of the alimentary canal has muscles that contract rhythmically to push food forward. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Peristalsis is the rhythmic, wave-like muscular contraction of the walls of the alimentary canal that pushes food along its length.

questions.question: During exhalation, exchange of gases takes place between:
options: Alveoli of the lungs and blood
Alveoli of the lungs and tissue fluid
questions.explanation: Gas exchange (of oxygen and carbon dioxide) always occurs between the alveoli of the lungs and the blood in the surrounding capillaries, regardless of whether the breath is being inhaled or exhaled.

questions.question: A plant is enclosed in a glass jar together with some lizards; a similar plant is enclosed in another jar without lizards. Both jars are kept under identical light conditions for a few hours. Which plant is likely to photosynthesise more, and why?

rubric.point: The plant enclosed WITH the lizards will photosynthesise more
Because the lizards respire, releasing extra carbon dioxide into the enclosed air, and this higher CO2 concentration allows a higher rate of photosynthesis in that jar

questions.model_answer: The plant enclosed together with the lizards is likely to photosynthesise more. The lizards' respiration releases additional carbon dioxide into the enclosed air of that jar, and since carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, this higher CO2 concentration supports a higher rate of photosynthesis than in the jar without lizards, where CO2 is only what the plant itself and any trapped air already contained.

questions.topic: Regulation of urine volume - osmotic balance
questions.question: The amount of urine produced generally decreases in summer compared to other seasons if a person doesn't stay sufficiently hydrated. Justify this observation.

rubric.point: Urine volume is regulated by selective reabsorption of water in the renal tubule of the nephron, depending on how much excess water the body has and how much dissolved waste needs to be excreted
In summer, more water is lost through sweating, so the body reabsorbs a greater proportion of the water filtered by the nephron to maintain osmotic balance, leaving less water to be excreted as urine

questions.model_answer: The amount of urine produced is controlled by selective reabsorption of water in the renal tubule of the nephron, which depends on how much excess water is present in the body versus how much dissolved waste needs to be excreted. In summer, more water is lost from the body through sweating, so the kidneys reabsorb a larger proportion of the water that was filtered, in order to maintain the body's osmotic balance - this leaves comparatively less water to be excreted, so urine output decreases if fluid intake isn't increased to compensate.

questions.topic: Structure of arteries suited to their function
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Arteries have thick, elastic walls.
Reason (R): Blood flows through arteries under high pressure, as they carry blood away from the heart to different organs of the body.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R explains A: since arteries must carry blood pumped directly by the heart, at high pressure, to various organs, their thick and elastic walls are structurally suited to withstand and accommodate that pressure without bursting.

questions.topic: Case study - the nephron and urine formation
questions.passage: Each human kidney contains millions of tiny filtration units called nephrons. Each nephron has a cup-shaped structure (Bowman's capsule) surrounding a cluster of blood capillaries (the glomerulus), which is connected to a long, coiled tubule. Blood entering the glomerulus under pressure is filtered here, and the filtrate then passes along the tubule, where useful substances are selectively reabsorbed back into the surrounding blood capillaries before the remaining fluid becomes urine.

subquestions.question: Name the filtration unit of the kidney described in the passage.

rubric.point: The nephron

subquestions.model_answer: This filtration unit is called the nephron.

subquestions.question: Name two substances that are useful to the body and are therefore selectively reabsorbed back into the blood as the filtrate passes along the tubule.

rubric.point: Useful substances reabsorbed include glucose, amino acids, salts (ions), and most of the water in the filtrate

subquestions.model_answer: Useful substances reabsorbed back into the blood include glucose and amino acids, along with most of the water and necessary salts (ions) - only substances the body doesn't need remain to be excreted as urine.

subquestions.question: Explain how the amount of water reabsorbed by the nephron helps regulate the overall volume and concentration of urine produced.

rubric.point: The amount of water reabsorbed depends on how much excess water is present in the body and how much dissolved waste needs to be excreted - if the body has excess water (e.g. after drinking a lot), less is reabsorbed and more dilute urine is produced; if the body needs to conserve water (e.g. in hot weather with heavy sweating), more water is reabsorbed, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine

subquestions.model_answer: The nephron regulates urine volume and concentration by adjusting how much water it reabsorbs from the filtrate, depending on the body's needs. If the body has more water than it needs (for instance after drinking plenty of fluids), less water is reabsorbed, and a larger volume of more dilute urine is produced. If the body needs to conserve water (for instance during hot weather with heavy sweating), the nephron reabsorbs a greater proportion of the filtered water, producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine - this selective reabsorption is how the kidneys maintain the body's overall water and osmotic balance.

notes.overview: This chapter explains how living organisms sense and respond to their environment through the nervous system (electrical signalling via neurons) and the endocrine system (chemical signalling via hormones), covering the structure of a neuron, reflex actions, the human brain, and hormone-based coordination in plants and animals.

sections.title: 1. The Neuron and Nerve Impulse
sections.content: A neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system, consisting of dendrites (which receive signals), a cell body with a nucleus, and a long axon (which transmits signals to the next neuron via a gap called a synapse). Information is received by dendrites, travels as an electrical impulse through the cell body and axon; at the synapse, the electrical signal triggers the release of chemicals (neurotransmitters) that cross the gap and start a new electrical signal in the adjacent neuron - this ensures the signal travels in one direction only.
sections.video_title: Signal Transmission - Control and Coordination (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 2. Reflex Actions and the Reflex Arc
sections.content: A reflex action is a sudden, automatic response to a stimulus that does not initially involve conscious thought, such as immediately withdrawing a hand upon touching a hot object; this rapid response is possible because the signal travels through a reflex arc, a pathway that connects the receptor to the effector via the spinal cord, without the need for information to first travel all the way to the brain. The pathway is: receptor (detects stimulus) -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord (relay/interneuron) -> motor neuron -> effector (muscle), allowing an extremely quick, protective response.

sections.title: 3. Human Brain: Structure and Functions
sections.content: The human brain is the main coordinating centre of the body, protected by the skull and a fluid-filled membrane called meninges, and is divided into three major regions: the forebrain (includes the cerebrum, the largest part, responsible for thinking, memory, voluntary actions, and interpretation of sensory information such as vision, hearing and smell), the midbrain (controls involuntary actions like the size of the pupil), and the hindbrain (includes the cerebellum, which maintains posture and balance and ensures precision of voluntary actions, and the medulla, which controls involuntary actions like blood pressure, salivation and vomiting).

sections.title: 4. Coordination in Plants: Tropisms and Plant Hormones
sections.content: Plants respond to stimuli through movement caused by growth, called tropic movements, which can be positive (growth towards the stimulus) or negative (growth away from it) - examples include phototropism (response to light, shoots are positively phototropic), geotropism (response to gravity, roots are positively geotropic), hydrotropism (response to water) and thigmotropism (response to touch, seen in tendrils of climbing plants). These growth movements are controlled by plant hormones: auxin (promotes cell elongation and is responsible for phototropic/geotropic bending), gibberellin (promotes stem growth), cytokinin (promotes cell division), and abscisic acid (inhibits growth and causes wilting, often called the stress hormone).

sections.title: 5. Coordination in Animals: Endocrine System and Hormones
sections.content: Animals use the endocrine system, consisting of ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, for chemical coordination that complements the faster nervous system - hormonal action tends to be slower but longer-lasting. Key human endocrine glands and their hormones include: the pituitary gland (the 'master gland', regulates growth and other glands), the thyroid gland (secretes thyroxine, which regulates metabolism and requires iodine - deficiency causes goitre), the pancreas (secretes insulin, which regulates blood sugar level - insufficient insulin causes diabetes), the adrenal glands (secrete adrenaline, the 'fight or flight' hormone, released during stress/excitement, increasing heartbeat and breathing rate), and the testes/ovaries (secrete sex hormones controlling changes during puberty).

key_terms.Neuron: The basic structural and functional unit of the nervous system that transmits nerve impulses.
key_terms.Synapse: The tiny gap between two neurons across which a nerve impulse is transmitted via neurotransmitter chemicals.
key_terms.Reflex arc: The neural pathway that controls a reflex action, from receptor through the spinal cord to the effector.
key_terms.Hormone: A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the bloodstream that regulates specific body functions.
key_terms.Tropism: The directional growth movement of a plant part in response to an external stimulus, such as light or gravity.

important_facts: Reflex arc pathway: receptor -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord -> motor neuron -> effector.
Cerebrum (forebrain) controls thinking and voluntary actions; cerebellum (hindbrain) controls balance and posture.
Auxin causes phototropic and geotropic bending in plants by promoting cell elongation.

questions.question: Compare nervous coordination and hormonal (chemical) coordination in animals.

Nervous coordination is fast and short-lived; hormonal coordination is slower but longer-lasting
Nervous system controls immediate actions (e.g. reflexes); hormones control long-term processes (e.g. growth, metabolism)

questions.model_answer: Nervous coordination works through electrical impulses transmitted by neurons and produces a fast, short-lived response, such as a reflex action. Hormonal coordination works through chemical messengers (hormones) released into the bloodstream by endocrine glands, producing a comparatively slower but longer-lasting effect. While the nervous system controls immediate, quick responses, the hormonal system regulates longer-term processes such as growth, metabolism and development.

Geotropism: growth movement in response to gravity; roots are positively geotropic (grow downward/towards gravity)

questions.model_answer: Phototropism is the growth movement of a plant part in response to light; shoots are positively phototropic and bend towards light. Geotropism is the growth movement in response to gravity; roots are positively geotropic and grow downward in the direction of gravity. Both these tropic movements are controlled by the plant hormone auxin, which causes unequal elongation of cells on opposite sides of the shoot or root, producing the bending response.

questions.question: Draw and explain the pathway of a reflex arc using a labelled example. Also describe the three main parts of the human brain and one function of each.

rubric.point: Reflex arc pathway: receptor detects stimulus -> sensory neuron -> spinal cord (relay neuron) -> motor neuron -> effector responds

questions.model_answer: In a reflex arc, a stimulus is detected by a receptor (e.g. skin sensing heat), which sends a signal through a sensory neuron to the spinal cord; here, a relay neuron passes the signal directly to a motor neuron, which carries it to an effector (a muscle), causing an immediate response such as withdrawing the hand from a hot object - all without the signal needing to first reach the brain, making the response very fast. The human brain has three main parts: the forebrain, which includes the cerebrum and is responsible for thinking, memory, voluntary actions and interpreting sensory information like vision and hearing; the midbrain, which controls certain involuntary actions such as the reflexes of the eye and ear (e.g. pupil size); and the hindbrain, which includes the cerebellum, responsible for maintaining posture and balance and ensuring precision of voluntary movements, and the medulla, which controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting.

questions.model_answer: A neuron has three main parts: dendrites, which receive signals from neighbouring neurons; a cell body containing the nucleus, which processes the incoming signal; and a long axon, which transmits the electrical impulse away from the cell body to the next neuron across a synapse.

questions.question: What are hydrotropism and thigmotropism? Give one example of each.

Thigmotropism is the growth movement in response to touch, e.g. tendrils of climbing plants coiling around a support

questions.model_answer: Adrenaline is a hormone secreted by the adrenal glands, released into the blood during moments of stress or excitement. It increases the heartbeat and breathing rate, diverting blood to the muscles, and prepares the body to respond quickly in a 'fight or flight' situation.

questions.question: What is the function of the midbrain, and give one example of an action it controls?

questions.model_answer: The midbrain, a part of the human brain located between the forebrain and hindbrain, controls certain involuntary actions of the body. For example, it controls reflexes of the eye and ear, such as adjusting the size of the pupil in response to light intensity.

questions.question: Explain how a nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another across a synapse, and why this transmission occurs in only one direction.

rubric.point: An electrical impulse travels along the dendrite, cell body and axon of a neuron
At the synapse, the impulse causes release of chemicals (neurotransmitters) which cross the gap
The neurotransmitters set off a new electrical signal in the next neuron; since they are released only from the axon end, transmission is unidirectional

questions.model_answer: Within a neuron, information travels as an electrical impulse from the dendrites through the cell body and along the axon. At the synapse, the gap between two neurons, this electrical impulse causes the release of chemicals called neurotransmitters, which diffuse across the gap and generate a new electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron. Since neurotransmitters are released only from the axon terminal of one neuron and received by the dendrite of the next, the nerve impulse can travel across a synapse in only one direction.

questions.question: State the functions of gibberellin, cytokinin and abscisic acid in plants.

Cytokinin promotes cell division, especially in fruits and seeds
Abscisic acid inhibits growth and causes wilting; acts as a stress hormone

questions.model_answer: Gibberellin is a plant hormone that promotes the growth and elongation of the stem. Cytokinin promotes cell division and is present in higher concentrations in regions of rapid cell division, such as fruits and seeds. Abscisic acid, often called the stress hormone, generally inhibits growth and causes wilting of leaves in response to stress conditions such as water scarcity.

questions.question: Explain the disorders caused by the deficiency or malfunctioning of the thyroid, pancreas and pituitary glands.

Pituitary: abnormal growth hormone secretion causes disorders like dwarfism (too little) or gigantism (too much)

questions.model_answer: If the thyroid gland does not receive enough iodine, it cannot make sufficient thyroxine, resulting in a disorder called goitre, where the thyroid gland swells up. If the pancreas does not secrete enough insulin, blood sugar levels rise, causing diabetes. Abnormal secretion of growth hormone by the pituitary gland can also cause disorders: too little growth hormone causes dwarfism (stunted growth), while too much can cause gigantism (excessive growth).

questions.question: Differentiate between voluntary, involuntary and reflex actions, giving one example of each.

questions.model_answer: Voluntary actions are performed consciously under the control of the cerebrum (forebrain), such as walking or writing. Involuntary actions occur automatically without conscious thought and are controlled mainly by the midbrain and hindbrain, such as heartbeat and breathing. Reflex actions are sudden, automatic responses to a stimulus that occur via the spinal cord without immediate involvement of the brain, such as instantly withdrawing the hand upon touching a hot object.

questions.question: Explain hydrotropism and thigmotropism with suitable examples, and state how these tropic movements benefit the plant.

rubric.point: Hydrotropism: growth in response to water; e.g. roots grow towards moist soil, helping the plant obtain water
Thigmotropism: growth in response to touch; e.g. tendrils coil around a support, helping climbing plants gain support
Both are examples of tropic (growth) movements that help the plant survive by responding directionally to environmental stimuli

questions.model_answer: Hydrotropism is the directional growth movement of roots towards a source of water, helping the plant obtain the moisture it needs. Thigmotropism is the directional growth movement in response to touch, seen in the tendrils of climbing plants, which coil around any support they come into contact with, helping the plant to climb and gain physical support. Both are tropic movements that allow the plant to respond and adapt to stimuli in its environment for better survival and growth.

questions.question: Describe the human endocrine system. Name at least four endocrine glands, the hormone(s) each secretes, and one function of each hormone.

rubric.point: Pituitary gland: regulates growth and controls other endocrine glands (master gland)
Thyroid gland: secretes thyroxine, regulates metabolism, requires iodine
Pancreas: secretes insulin, regulates blood sugar level
Adrenal glands: secrete adrenaline, prepares body for fight or flight (increases heartbeat/breathing)
Testes/ovaries: secrete sex hormones controlling changes during puberty

questions.model_answer: The endocrine system consists of ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream for chemical coordination. The pituitary gland, called the master gland, regulates body growth and controls the activity of several other endocrine glands. The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine, which regulates carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism, and requires iodine for its synthesis. The pancreas secretes insulin, which regulates blood sugar levels; insufficient insulin causes diabetes. The adrenal glands secrete adrenaline, the 'fight or flight' hormone, which is released during stress and increases heartbeat and breathing rate. The testes in males and ovaries in females secrete sex hormones that bring about the physical changes seen during puberty.

questions.question: What are tropic movements in plants? Explain phototropism and geotropism with examples, and describe the role of auxin, gibberellin and cytokinin in plant growth.

rubric.point: Tropic movements are directional growth movements of a plant part towards or away from a stimulus
Phototropism: growth in response to light; shoots are positively phototropic
Geotropism: growth in response to gravity; roots are positively geotropic
Auxin causes unequal cell elongation responsible for phototropic/geotropic bending
Gibberellin promotes stem growth; cytokinin promotes cell division

questions.model_answer: Tropic movements are directional growth movements of a plant part, either towards (positive) or away from (negative) a stimulus. Phototropism is the growth movement in response to light; shoots are positively phototropic and bend towards the light source. Geotropism is the growth movement in response to gravity; roots are positively geotropic and grow downward into the soil. These bending movements are caused by the plant hormone auxin, which accumulates on the side away from the stimulus and causes unequal elongation of cells, producing the characteristic bend. Besides auxin, gibberellin promotes the growth and elongation of the stem, while cytokinin promotes cell division, particularly in areas of rapid growth such as fruits and seeds.

questions.topic: Case study - adrenaline and the 'fight or flight' response
questions.passage: When a person is suddenly frightened, the adrenal glands release the hormone adrenaline directly into the bloodstream. This hormone prepares the body to deal with the emergency by acting on several organs at once: it increases the heartbeat (supplying more oxygen to the muscles), redirects blood flow away from the digestive system towards the skeletal muscles, and increases the breathing rate.

subquestions.question: Adrenaline is secreted by which gland?

subquestions.question: Explain how adrenaline prepares the body's circulatory and respiratory systems to respond to danger.

subquestions.model_answer: Adrenaline increases the heartbeat, which pumps more oxygenated blood to the skeletal muscles. It also increases the breathing rate by acting on the diaphragm and rib muscles, supplying more oxygen, and redirects blood flow away from the digestive system towards the muscles - together preparing the body for quick action ('fight or flight').

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.topic: One hormone acting on multiple organs
questions.question: In animals, a hormone secreted by one organ can act on multiple other organs. Justify this statement by explaining the effect of a single animal hormone on three different organs.

questions.model_answer: Adrenaline, secreted by the adrenal glands, is a good example of a single hormone acting on multiple organs as part of the body's 'fight or flight' response: it acts on the sweat glands to increase sweat production, it acts on the heart to increase the rate and force of its contractions (improving oxygen delivery to the muscles), and it acts on the blood vessels supplying the digestive system, constricting them so blood is diverted away from digestion and towards organs more urgently needed in an emergency.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A nerve impulse at a synapse always travels from the axonal end of one neuron to the dendritic end of the next neuron, not in the reverse direction.
Reason (R): Chemicals are released only at the axonal end of a neuron, and only these chemicals can cross the synaptic gap to generate a new electrical impulse in the dendrite of the next neuron.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.question: Name the plant hormones responsible for each of the following effects: (a) elongation of cells, (b) promotion of cell division, (c) inhibition of growth and promotion of falling of senescent (mature/ageing) leaves.

questions.subject: biology

notes.overview: This chapter explains why reproduction is essential for the continuation of a species, describes the various modes of asexual reproduction seen in simple organisms, explains sexual reproduction in flowering plants and in humans (including the male and female reproductive systems and the menstrual cycle), and covers reproductive health, including contraception and sexually transmitted infections.

sections.title: 1. Importance of Reproduction
sections.content: Reproduction is the biological process by which living organisms produce new individuals of their own kind, ensuring the continuation of a species across generations. Unlike processes such as nutrition or respiration, reproduction is not essential for the survival of an individual organism, but it is essential for the survival of the species as a whole; reproduction also introduces variations, which provide the raw material for evolution and help a population adapt to changing environments.
sections.video_title: Do Organisms Create Exact Copies of Themselves? (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 2. Modes of Asexual Reproduction
sections.content: Asexual reproduction involves a single parent producing offspring that are genetically identical (clones) to the parent, without the fusion of gametes. Common types include: fission (a unicellular organism like Amoeba splitting into two, or Plasmodium undergoing multiple fission); budding (a small outgrowth called a bud develops on the parent and eventually detaches, as in Hydra and yeast); fragmentation (the body breaks into pieces, each of which regenerates into a new organism, as in Spirogyra); regeneration (a organism regrows a lost or damaged body part from specialised cells, as in Planaria); and vegetative propagation (new plants grow from vegetative parts like roots, stems or leaves, as in the eyes of a potato tuber or leaves of Bryophyllum).

sections.title: 3. Vegetative Propagation and Tissue Culture
sections.content: Vegetative propagation allows new plants to be grown artificially from parts of a parent plant, using methods like cutting, layering and grafting; plants grown this way are genetically identical to the parent and can bear fruit/flowers earlier than plants grown from seeds, and can preserve desirable characteristics that might otherwise be lost through sexual reproduction (which is useful, e.g., for seedless varieties). Tissue culture is a modern technique in which a small piece of plant tissue is grown in a nutrient medium under sterile laboratory conditions to rapidly produce genetically identical plantlets.

sections.title: 4. Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
sections.content: A flower is the reproductive organ of a plant, and typically contains the male reproductive part, the stamen (consisting of anther, which produces pollen grains, and filament), and the female reproductive part, the pistil/carpel (consisting of stigma, style, and ovary, which contains ovules). Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma - self-pollination (within the same flower) or cross-pollination (between different flowers, aided by wind, water, or insects). After pollination, the pollen grain forms a pollen tube that grows down through the style to reach the ovule, where fertilisation occurs - the fusion of the male and female gametes to form a zygote, which develops into an embryo; the ovule develops into a seed, and the ovary develops into a fruit.

sections.title: 5. Male Reproductive System in Humans
sections.content: The male reproductive system includes a pair of testes (located in the scrotum, outside the abdominal cavity, since sperm production requires a slightly lower temperature than body temperature), which produce sperm (male gametes) and the hormone testosterone (which brings about changes in appearance during puberty); the vas deferens carries sperm from the testes, joined by secretions from glands like the seminal vesicles and prostate gland, which nourish and provide a fluid medium for the sperm, forming semen, which is delivered through the urethra during ejaculation.

sections.title: 6. Female Reproductive System and Menstrual Cycle
sections.content: The female reproductive system includes a pair of ovaries (which produce eggs/ova and the hormone estrogen), fallopian tubes (oviducts, where fertilisation of the egg by sperm normally occurs), and the uterus (where a fertilised egg implants and develops into a foetus during pregnancy, connected to the outside via the cervix and vagina). The menstrual cycle is a roughly monthly cycle in which the uterine lining thickens in preparation for a possible pregnancy; if fertilisation does not occur, this thickened lining, along with blood, is shed through the vagina - a process called menstruation, which typically lasts about 28 days.

sections.title: 7. Fertilisation, Pregnancy and Childbirth
sections.content: Fertilisation occurs when a sperm fuses with an egg in the fallopian tube, forming a zygote, which undergoes repeated cell division as it travels toward the uterus and implants in the uterine lining, developing into an embryo and then a foetus. The developing foetus is nourished and protected via the placenta, a specialised tissue that allows the exchange of nutrients, oxygen and waste products between the mother's blood and the foetus's blood (without the two bloods actually mixing). Human pregnancy typically lasts about 9 months (38-40 weeks), after which childbirth occurs through hormonally induced contractions of the uterus.

sections.title: 8. Reproductive Health - Contraception
sections.content: Contraception refers to methods used to prevent pregnancy, broadly classified as: barrier methods (like condoms, which physically prevent sperm from reaching the egg, and also help prevent the spread of sexually transmitted infections); chemical methods (like oral contraceptive pills, which alter hormonal balance to prevent ovulation); intrauterine devices (like copper-T, which prevent implantation); and surgical methods (like vasectomy in males and tubectomy in females, which block the pathways for sperm/egg transport, generally considered permanent).

sections.title: 9. Sexually Transmitted Infections (STIs)
sections.content: Sexually transmitted infections (STIs) are infections spread primarily through sexual contact, including bacterial infections like gonorrhoea and syphilis (treatable with antibiotics) and viral infections like HIV-AIDS and genital warts/herpes (not curable by antibiotics, though some are manageable/preventable). Using barrier methods like condoms during sexual contact substantially reduces the risk of transmission of most STIs.

key_terms.Asexual reproduction: Reproduction involving a single parent, producing genetically identical offspring, without gamete fusion.
key_terms.Pollination: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower.
key_terms.Fertilisation: The fusion of a male gamete (sperm/pollen) and a female gamete (egg/ovule) to form a zygote.
key_terms.Placenta: A specialised tissue connecting the foetus to the uterine wall, enabling exchange of nutrients, oxygen and waste between mother and foetus.
key_terms.Menstruation: The periodic shedding of the thickened uterine lining and blood when fertilisation does not occur, roughly every 28 days.
key_terms.Contraception: Methods used to prevent pregnancy, including barrier, chemical, intrauterine and surgical methods.

questions.model_answer: Pollination is the first step, in which pollen grains are transferred from the anther to the stigma of a flower, either through self-pollination (same flower) or cross-pollination (different flowers, aided by agents like wind, water or insects). After landing on a compatible stigma, the pollen grain germinates and forms a pollen tube, which grows down through the style and enters the ovule inside the ovary. Fertilisation then occurs when the male gamete carried by the pollen tube fuses with the egg cell within the ovule, forming a zygote. Following fertilisation, the ovule develops into a seed (containing the developing embryo), and the ovary develops into a fruit that encloses and protects the seed(s).

questions.model_answer: The male reproductive system consists of a pair of testes, located in the scrotum outside the abdominal cavity (since sperm production requires a slightly lower temperature than the rest of the body), which produce sperm and secrete the hormone testosterone, responsible for changes in appearance during puberty. Sperm produced in the testes travel through the vas deferens toward the urethra. questions.model_answer: The female reproductive system consists of a pair of ovaries, which produce eggs (ova) and secrete the hormone estrogen. Each ovary is connected to a fallopian tube (oviduct), through which a released egg travels toward the uterus, and it is normally within the fallopian tube that fertilisation of the egg by a sperm occurs. questions.model_answer: During each menstrual cycle, the lining of the uterus thickens and becomes richly supplied with blood vessels, preparing it to receive and nourish a fertilised egg in case pregnancy occurs. If fertilisation does not occur, this thickened lining is no longer needed, so it breaks down and is shed, along with some blood, through the vagina - this shedding is called menstruation, and the cycle then begins again, typically repeating about every 28 days. If fertilisation does occur, the resulting embryo travels to the uterus and implants itself into the thickened lining; in this case, menstruation does not occur, and the uterine lining is instead maintained and further developed over the following months to nourish and support the growing embryo and foetus throughout pregnancy.

questions.question: Classify contraceptive methods into four broad categories, giving one example of each.

questions.model_answer: Contraceptive methods can be broadly classified into four categories. Barrier methods, such as condoms, physically prevent sperm from reaching the egg, and also help reduce the spread of sexually transmitted infections. Chemical methods, such as oral contraceptive pills, work by altering hormonal balance to prevent ovulation. Intrauterine devices, such as the copper-T, are inserted into the uterus and work mainly by preventing implantation of a fertilised egg. Surgical methods, such as vasectomy in males (blocking the vas deferens) and tubectomy in females (blocking the fallopian tubes), physically block the pathways needed for sperm or egg transport and are generally considered permanent.

questions.question: Describe five different modes of asexual reproduction, giving one example organism for each.

rubric.point: Fission: splitting of a unicellular organism into two (or more) daughter cells, e.g. Amoeba
Budding: a small outgrowth develops and detaches as a new individual, e.g. Hydra/yeast
Fragmentation: the body breaks into pieces, each regenerating into a new organism, e.g. Spirogyra
Regeneration: regrowth of a lost body part from specialised cells, e.g. Planaria
Vegetative propagation: new plants grow from vegetative parts, e.g. potato tuber eyes / Bryophyllum leaves

questions.model_answer: Several modes of asexual reproduction are seen across simple organisms. Fission is the splitting of a unicellular organism into two (or more) genetically identical daughter cells, as seen in Amoeba. Budding involves a small outgrowth (bud) developing on the parent's body, which grows and eventually detaches as a new, independent individual, as seen in Hydra and in yeast. Fragmentation occurs when the body of an organism breaks into several pieces, each of which is capable of regenerating into a complete new organism, as seen in Spirogyra. Regeneration is the ability of an organism to regrow a lost or damaged body part from specialised cells, notably demonstrated by Planaria, which can regenerate an entire new individual from just a fragment of its body. Vegetative propagation is seen in plants, where new individuals grow from vegetative parts such as roots, stems, or leaves - for example, new potato plants growing from the 'eyes' of a potato tuber, or new plantlets growing from the notches along the leaf margins of Bryophyllum.

questions.topic: Human reproductive process - fertilisation to birth
questions.question: Describe the process of human reproduction from fertilisation through to childbirth, including the role of the placenta.

rubric.point: Fertilisation occurs in the fallopian tube when a sperm fuses with an egg, forming a zygote
The zygote undergoes repeated cell divisions as it travels to the uterus and implants in the uterine lining, developing into an embryo
Placenta forms and connects the developing embryo/foetus to the uterine wall, enabling exchange of nutrients, oxygen and waste between mother and foetus without their blood mixing directly
keywords: placenta exchange nutrients oxygen waste no mixing

rubric.point: The embryo develops into a foetus over the course of pregnancy, which lasts about 9 months (38-40 weeks) in humans
Childbirth occurs through hormonally induced, rhythmic contractions of the uterus that push the baby out through the vagina

questions.model_answer: Human reproduction begins with fertilisation, which occurs in the fallopian tube when a sperm fuses with an egg to form a single-celled zygote. This zygote undergoes repeated cell divisions as it travels down the fallopian tube toward the uterus, and by the time it reaches the uterus, it implants itself into the thickened uterine lining, where it continues to develop into an embryo. During this development, the placenta forms - a specialised tissue connecting the embryo (and later, the foetus) to the wall of the uterus via the umbilical cord. The placenta enables the exchange of nutrients, oxygen and waste products between the mother's blood and the foetus's blood, without the two blood supplies actually mixing directly, allowing the foetus to receive nourishment and eliminate waste throughout development. Over the course of pregnancy, which lasts approximately 9 months (38 to 40 weeks) in humans, the embryo develops into a fully formed foetus. At the end of pregnancy, childbirth occurs through hormonally induced, rhythmic contractions of the muscular walls of the uterus, which gradually push the baby out through the cervix and vagina.

questions.model_answer: Vegetative propagation is a form of asexual reproduction in which a new plant develops from a vegetative part of the parent plant - such as a root, stem, or leaf - rather than from a seed. questions.model_answer: Preventing sexually transmitted infections (STIs) is important because untreated infections can cause serious reproductive health problems, infertility, and in some cases (such as HIV-AIDS), can be life-threatening. Two methods that help prevent STIs are: (1) using barrier methods such as condoms during sexual intercourse, which prevent the exchange of bodily fluids, and (2) avoiding unprotected sexual contact with infected individuals and maintaining a single, mutually faithful partner.

questions.topic: Comprehensive - modes of reproduction and their significance
questions.question: (a) Why is variation important for a species? (b) How does sexual reproduction, compared to asexual reproduction, contribute to variation? (c) Briefly describe the role of DNA copying in reproduction.

rubric.point: (a) Variation helps a species survive changing environmental conditions - some variants may survive events that others cannot
(b) Sexual reproduction combines DNA from two parents, creating greater genetic variation than asexual reproduction (which produces near-identical clones)
(c) DNA copying is not always exact; small variations (errors) during copying are the basic source of new variation, which is essential for evolution

questions.model_answer: (a) Variation is important because it increases the chances that at least some individuals of a species will survive changes in the environment (such as disease, climate change, or new predators) that could otherwise wipe out the entire population. (b) Sexual reproduction combines genetic material (DNA) from two different parents, producing offspring with a unique combination of traits, leading to much greater variation than asexual reproduction, which produces offspring that are nearly identical copies (clones) of a single parent. (c) During reproduction, the DNA blueprint of the parent(s) is copied and passed on to the offspring; this copying process is not always perfectly accurate, and small variations (errors) that occur become the basic source of new variation in a population, providing the raw material on which evolution acts over generations.

questions.topic: Emasculation to promote cross-pollination and improve yield
questions.question: Ravi cultivated mustard (a plant with bisexual flowers) on his farm. His plants were diseased, due to a gene defect, and had reduced yield. Ravi removed the stamens from the diseased plants, and also planted fresh disease-free mustard plants where he removed the pistils. How will this strategy help improve the yield of mustard?

rubric.point: Removing the stamens from the diseased (bisexual) flowers converts them to functionally female flowers, forcing cross-pollination instead of self-pollination
Cross-pollination between the diseased and disease-free plants increases genetic variation in the offspring, improving the chances of disease-free, higher-yielding progeny

questions.model_answer: By removing the stamens from the diseased plants, Ravi turned their bisexual flowers into functionally female flowers, which can no longer self-pollinate and must instead receive pollen from another plant (cross-pollination) - in this case, from the disease-free plants whose pistils he removed to make them functionally male pollen donors. This forced cross-pollination increases genetic variation among the offspring, raising the chance that the resulting seeds carry the disease-free trait and give a healthier, higher-yielding crop than continued self-pollination of the diseased plants would.

rubric.point: Regeneration: if an organism is cut/broken into pieces, many of the pieces can grow into complete new individuals, since some of their cells behave like stem cells and can differentiate into all needed cell types
Budding: a small outgrowth (bud) forms on the parent organism from a cluster of actively dividing cells, and eventually detaches to grow into a new individual
Testes and ovaries are functionally similar - both are the primary sex organs that produce gametes (sperm/eggs) and secrete the sex hormones that drive reproductive development

questions.model_answer: Two modes of asexual reproduction that resemble what stem cells do are regeneration and budding. In regeneration, if an organism such as Planaria is cut or broken into several pieces, many of those pieces - because they retain undifferentiated, stem-cell-like cells - can grow into complete new individuals. In budding (seen in Hydra), a cluster of rapidly dividing cells forms a small outgrowth or bud on the parent's body, which develops its own structures and eventually detaches to live as an independent new individual - in both cases, as with stem cells, undifferentiated cells divide and differentiate to build new structures. Two pairs of functionally analogous reproductive organs are: the testes and ovaries, both of which are the primary sex organs, producing gametes (sperm and eggs respectively) and secreting the sex hormones responsible for reproductive development; and the vas deferens and the fallopian tube, both of which are ducts whose job is to carry a gamete (sperm, or the released egg) towards the site where fertilisation takes place.
