notes.overview: This chapter explains how traits are passed from parents to offspring, introduces Mendel's foundational experiments on pea plants that revealed the basic rules of inheritance, explains dominant and recessive traits, genotype and phenotype, and describes how sex is determined in humans, along with the concept of variation as the raw material for evolution.

sections.title: 1. Variation and Heredity
sections.content: Variation refers to the differences in characteristics/traits seen among individuals of the same species, arising during reproduction due to errors or inaccuracies in the DNA copying process during cell division, and also due to the reshuffling of genes during sexual reproduction. Heredity is the process by which characteristics/traits are transmitted from parents to their offspring, through genes carried on chromosomes present in the reproductive cells (gametes).

sections.title: 2. Mendel's Experiments - Monohybrid Cross
sections.content: Gregor Mendel, working with pea plants, crossed a pure-bred tall plant (TT) with a pure-bred short plant (tt) and observed that all offspring in the first generation (F1) were tall, showing that the 'tall' trait is dominant over the 'short' (recessive) trait. When these F1 tall plants were self-pollinated, the second generation (F2) showed both tall and short plants in an approximate ratio of 3:1, showing that the recessive 'short' trait, though hidden in F1, was not lost and reappeared in F2.
sections.video_title: Rule for the Inheritance of Traits - Monohybrid Cross (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 3. Dominant and Recessive Traits, Genotype and Phenotype
sections.content: A dominant trait is one that expresses itself even when only one copy of the gene (allele) for it is present (e.g. Tt shows the tall phenotype); a recessive trait expresses itself only when both copies of the gene are present in the recessive form (e.g. tt shows the short phenotype). The genotype of an organism refers to its actual genetic makeup (e.g. TT, Tt, or tt), while the phenotype refers to its observable physical characteristics (e.g. tall or short) - organisms with different genotypes (TT and Tt) can have the same phenotype (both tall).
keywords: dominant trait expresses with one allele
sections.video_title: Mendel's Findings - Law of Dominance and Segregation (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 4. Mendel's Experiments - Dihybrid Cross
sections.content: Mendel also crossed pea plants differing in two traits simultaneously (e.g. seed shape - round/wrinkled, and seed colour - yellow/green), finding that these two traits are inherited independently of each other, a principle now known as the law of independent assortment; the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross shows four phenotype combinations in an approximate ratio of 9:3:3:1, demonstrating that the inheritance of one trait does not affect the inheritance of another.

sections.title: 5. Sex Determination in Humans
sections.content: Human somatic cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total), including 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes: females have two X chromosomes (XX), while males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). Since all eggs produced by a female carry an X chromosome, while sperm produced by a male carry either an X or a Y chromosome in roughly equal numbers, the sex of a child is determined by which type of sperm fertilises the egg: an X-carrying sperm results in a girl (XX), while a Y-carrying sperm results in a boy (XY) - meaning the father's chromosome contribution determines the child's sex.

sections.title: 6. How Traits are Inherited - Rules Summary
sections.content: From Mendel's monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, two key rules of inheritance emerge: the law of dominance, which states that when two contrasting alleles are present together (heterozygous), only the dominant one is expressed in the phenotype, while the recessive one remains hidden but is still present in the genotype; and the law of independent assortment, which states that different traits (controlled by genes on different chromosomes) are inherited independently of one another.
sections.video_title: How Do These Traits Get Expressed? (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 7. Variation as Raw Material for Evolution
sections.content: Variations arising during reproduction are not evenly useful - some variations may be advantageous to an organism in a particular environment (helping it survive and reproduce more successfully), while others may be neutral or harmful. Organisms with advantageous variations are more likely to survive and pass those variations on to their offspring, a process that, accumulated over many generations, drives evolutionary change and helps explain the diversity of life adapted to different environments.
keywords: survival and reproduction of favourable variants

sections.title: 8. Acquired vs Inherited Traits
sections.content: Inherited traits are those passed from parents to offspring through genes present in the germ cells (gametes), and can be passed on to future generations (e.g. eye colour, blood group). Acquired traits are changes that occur in an individual's body during its lifetime due to environmental influences or use/disuse (e.g. a well-developed muscle from exercise, or a scar from an injury), and generally cannot be passed on to offspring since they do not alter the DNA of the germ cells.
keywords: acquired traits during lifetime not passed on

sections.title: 9. Applications of Heredity - Sex Ratio Awareness
sections.content: Understanding that the sex of a child is determined by the father's sperm (contributing either an X or Y chromosome) rather than anything about the mother is scientifically important for dispelling harmful social myths that blame women for the sex of their child; awareness of this genetic reality has social and legal significance (prenatal sex determination for the purpose of sex-selective practices is illegal in India under the PCPNDT Act).
keywords: father's chromosome determines sex not mother

key_terms.Gene: A unit of heredity, made of DNA, that carries information for a particular trait.
key_terms.Dominant trait: A trait that is expressed in the phenotype even when only one copy of its allele is present.

Not every variation is equally useful to an organism - in a given environment, some variations may provide a survival advantage, helping an organism survive and reproduce more successfully than others with less favourable variations, while other variations may be neutral or even harmful. Organisms carrying advantageous variations tend to survive longer and produce more offspring, passing these favourable traits on to the next generation more frequently. Accumulated over many generations, this process - natural selection acting on variation - gradually shifts the characteristics of a population, driving evolutionary change and helping species become better adapted to their environments over time.

questions.question: Describe Mendel's monohybrid and dihybrid cross experiments on pea plants, stating the two laws of inheritance that emerged from these experiments.

questions.model_answer: In his monohybrid cross experiment, Mendel crossed a pure-breeding tall pea plant (TT) with a pure-breeding short pea plant (tt). All F1 offspring were tall (Tt), showing tallness is dominant. When F1 plants were self-pollinated, the F2 generation showed tall and short plants in an approximate 3:1 ratio, showing the recessive short trait reappeared. In his dihybrid cross experiment, Mendel crossed pea plants differing in two traits simultaneously - for example, round yellow seeds crossed with wrinkled green seeds. The F2 generation showed all four possible combinations of these traits (round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow, wrinkled green) in an approximate ratio of 9:3:3:1, showing that the two traits were inherited independently of one another. From these two sets of experiments, Mendel established two foundational laws of inheritance: the law of dominance, which states that when two contrasting alleles for a trait are present together, only the dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype, while the recessive allele remains hidden but is retained in the genotype; and the law of independent assortment, which states that different traits, controlled by genes on different chromosomes, are inherited independently of each other. Together, these two laws, derived from careful experimentation and mathematical analysis of ratios, laid the foundation for the modern science of genetics.

Mendel crossed pure-bred pea plants with round, yellow seeds against pure-bred plants with wrinkled, green seeds. In the F2 generation, he observed a phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1 - that is, 9 round-yellow : 3 round-green : 3 wrinkled-yellow : 1 wrinkled-green - showing that the two traits (seed shape and seed colour) are inherited independently of each other.

questions.question: What is speciation? Name two factors that can lead to the formation of a new species.

rubric.point: Speciation is the process by which a new species forms, usually from an existing population that becomes isolated
Factor 1: geographical isolation, which prevents gene flow between separated populations
Factor 2: genetic drift and/or accumulation of variations over many generations leading to reproductive isolation

questions.model_answer: Speciation is the evolutionary process by which a new species is formed, typically when a population becomes isolated from the rest of its species and accumulates enough genetic differences over time that its members can no longer interbreed with the original population. Two factors that can lead to speciation are: (1) geographical isolation, such as a mountain range or river separating a population, which prevents gene flow between the separated groups, and (2) genetic drift, where random changes in the frequency of variations accumulate differently in the isolated populations over many generations, eventually leading to reproductive isolation.

questions.question: Explain why the sex of a child is determined by the father's chromosome contribution and not the mother's, in humans.

rubric.point: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, one pair being the sex chromosomes: XX in females and XY in males
The mother always contributes an X chromosome (since she only has X chromosomes)
The father contributes either an X or a Y chromosome (50% chance each), so his contribution determines whether the child is XX (female) or XY (male)
keywords: father's X or Y determines sex

questions.model_answer: In humans, one of the 23 pairs of chromosomes is the sex chromosome pair: females have two X chromosomes (XX), while males have one X and one Y chromosome (XY). Since the mother only has X chromosomes, every egg cell she produces carries an X chromosome - her contribution is always the same. The father, however, produces sperm carrying either an X or a Y chromosome with equal (50%) probability. It is this variable contribution from the father that determines the sex of the child: an X from the father results in an XX (female) child, while a Y results in an XY (male) child.

questions.question: Distinguish between acquired traits and inherited traits, giving one example of each, and explain why acquired traits are not passed on to offspring.

rubric.point: Inherited traits are passed from parents to offspring through genes (DNA), e.g. eye colour
Acquired traits develop during an individual's lifetime due to environment/use, e.g. a well-developed muscle from exercise
Acquired traits do not alter the DNA of germ cells (reproductive cells), so they cannot be inherited by the next generation
keywords: do not alter germ cell DNA

questions.model_answer: Inherited traits are characteristics passed from parents to offspring through genes carried on DNA, such as eye colour or blood group. Acquired traits, on the other hand, develop in an individual during their own lifetime as a result of environmental factors or use, such as a well-developed muscle from regular exercise. Acquired traits are not passed on to offspring because they do not cause any change in the DNA of the germ cells (sperm or egg cells) - only changes in an organism's genetic material can be inherited by the next generation.

questions.question: (a) State Mendel's law of dominance. (b) In a monohybrid cross between a pure-bred tall pea plant (TT) and a pure-bred short pea plant (tt), what will be the genotype and phenotype of the F1 generation? (c) If the F1 plants are self-pollinated, what genotypic and phenotypic ratios are expected in the F2 generation?

rubric.point: (a) Law of dominance: when two contrasting alleles are present together, only the dominant allele expresses itself in the phenotype, while the recessive allele is masked
(b) F1 genotype is Tt (heterozygous); phenotype is tall (since T is dominant)
(c) F2 genotypic ratio 1:2:1 (TT:Tt:tt); phenotypic ratio 3:1 (tall:short)

questions.model_answer: (a) Mendel's law of dominance states that when two contrasting alleles (forms of a gene) for a trait are present together in an organism, only the dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype, while the recessive allele remains masked/unexpressed. (b) Crossing a pure tall plant (TT) with a pure short plant (tt) produces F1 offspring that are all Tt (heterozygous) in genotype; since tallness (T) is dominant, all F1 plants are tall in phenotype. (c) When F1 (Tt) plants are self-pollinated, the F2 generation shows a genotypic ratio of 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, and a phenotypic ratio of 3 tall : 1 short.

questions.topic: Comprehensive - evidence and mechanism of evolution
questions.question: (a) What is evolution? (b) Explain how fossils provide evidence for evolution. (c) How does natural selection act as a mechanism driving evolutionary change?

rubric.point: (a) Evolution is the gradual change in heritable characteristics of a population over successive generations

(b) Fossils are preserved remains/impressions of ancient organisms found in rock layers; older fossils (deeper/simpler layers) compared to younger ones (more complex) show a record of gradual change over time

(c) Natural selection: individuals with variations better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing those variations to offspring, so favourable variations accumulate over generations

questions.model_answer: (a) Evolution is the gradual change in the heritable characteristics of a population of organisms over successive generations, leading over long periods of time to the emergence of new species. (b) Fossils are the preserved remains or impressions of organisms that lived in the past, found embedded in layers of rock. By studying fossils found in different rock layers (strata), scientists can see how organisms have changed over time - simpler or more ancient forms are typically found in deeper/older rock layers, while more complex or modern forms appear in more recent layers, providing a record of gradual evolutionary change. (c) Natural selection acts as a mechanism for evolution because, within a population, individuals show natural variation; those individuals whose variations make them better suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce successfully. Since these advantageous variations are passed on to their offspring, they gradually become more common in the population over many generations, driving evolutionary change.

questions.topic: Monohybrid cross - predicting parental genotypes from offspring ratio
questions.question: In cattle, having horns is a recessive trait (h) compared to not having horns (H). When cattle with horns are crossed with cattle without horns, the offspring show a 1:1 ratio of horned to hornless. Which of the following is MOST LIKELY true of the parents?
questions.explanation: The horned parent must be hh (recessive trait requires two recessive alleles). A 1:1 ratio of horned (hh) to hornless offspring results from crossing hh with a heterozygous Hh hornless parent (Hh x hh -> 1 Hh : 1 hh) - so the hornless parent must be heterozygous.

questions.topic: Monohybrid self-cross - gamete and offspring percentages
questions.question: If two pea plants having round and green seeds, both of genotype RrGg, are crossed with each other, identify the percentage of the following in the F1 generation of this cross: (a) gametes carrying both the round (R) and yellow (G... use dominant yellow allele) seed-colour alleles together, (b) offspring having the same genotype as the parents (RrGg), (c) offspring having the same phenotype as the parents (round, green... i.e. round and yellow, matching the dominant phenotypes).

rubric.point: Each RrGg parent produces four types of gametes in equal proportion (RG, Rg, rG, rg), so gametes carrying both dominant alleles together (RG) make up 25% of the gametes
In a dihybrid self-cross (RrGg x RrGg), the fraction of offspring with the same heterozygous genotype as the parents (RrGg) is 4/16 = 25%
The fraction of offspring showing the same phenotype as the parents (dominant for both traits, i.e. round and the dominant seed-colour) is 9/16, which is 56.25%

questions.model_answer: An RrGg plant produces four types of gametes in equal 1:1:1:1 proportion - RG, Rg, rG and rg - so gametes carrying both dominant alleles together (RG) make up 25% of all gametes. In a self-cross of two RrGg plants (a standard dihybrid cross), the offspring genotypes follow the familiar 9:3:3:1 phenotypic pattern derived from 16 equally likely genotype combinations; among these, exactly 4 out of 16 combinations give the heterozygous RrGg genotype matching the parents, i.e. 25%. The offspring showing the same phenotype as the parents (dominant for both traits) make up 9 out of 16 combinations, i.e. 56.25%.

Reason (R): Variations can be caused due to inaccurate copying of DNA during reproduction.

questions.topic: Case study - inheritance pattern of an autosomal recessive trait (sickle cell anaemia)
questions.passage:
Ram and Asha are a married couple with several children. One of their children has sickle cell anaemia, while the others show no symptoms of the condition. Neither Ram nor Asha shows any symptoms of sickle cell anaemia themselves. The gene for sickle cell anaemia is located on an autosome (it is not linked to the sex chromosomes).

Note: this case study's source marking scheme contained an unrelated answer (about X-linked colour blindness) that does not match this question as printed - the analysis below has been independently worked out from the actual sickle-cell scenario described here, using standard autosomal-recessive inheritance.

subquestions.question: Is sickle cell anaemia, in this family, caused by a dominant or a recessive allele? Explain your reasoning.

rubric.point: It is caused by a recessive allele
Because both parents are phenotypically unaffected, yet they had a child who is affected - this is only possible if the trait is recessive and both parents are unaffected heterozygous carriers

subquestions.model_answer: It is a recessive allele. Since neither Ram nor Asha shows symptoms of sickle cell anaemia, yet they have a child who does, both parents must be carrying the affected allele without expressing it themselves - which is only possible if the trait is recessive and both parents are unaffected heterozygous carriers.

subquestions.question: Using S for the normal (dominant) allele and s for the sickle-cell (recessive) allele, identify the genotypes of Ram and Asha. If their affected child (genotype ss) grows up and marries a person with no mutation in the sickle-cell gene (genotype SS), what percentage of their children would be expected to have sickle cell anaemia? Show the cross.

rubric.point: Ram and Asha are both unaffected carriers, genotype Ss
Cross ss (affected child) x SS (unaffected, no mutation) gives all offspring genotype Ss - all phenotypically unaffected carriers
Therefore 0% of their children would have sickle cell anaemia (though 100% would be carriers)

subquestions.model_answer: Since sickle cell anaemia is recessive and both unaffected parents had an affected child, Ram and Asha must both be genotype Ss (unaffected carriers). If their affected child (ss) marries someone with no mutation in the gene at all (SS), the cross ss x SS gives: all gametes from the ss parent are s, and all gametes from the SS parent are S, so every offspring is Ss. All of their children would therefore be phenotypically unaffected (but 100% would be carriers) - so 0% of their children would actually have sickle cell anaemia.

Assertion (A): The sex of a child is determined by which sex chromosome it inherits from its mother.
Reason (R): In humans, every egg produced by the mother carries an X chromosome, while sperm produced by the father can carry either an X or a Y chromosome.

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.

R is true and correctly describes the underlying biology, even though it does not support A as worded (it actually explains why the FATHER, not the mother, determines the child's sex).

questions.topic: Homologous versus analogous structures as evidence for evolution
questions.question: Distinguish between homologous and analogous structures, giving one example of each, and explain how homologous structures provide evidence for evolution.

rubric.point: Homologous structures have the same basic structural design/origin but may serve different functions in different organisms (e.g. the forelimbs of humans, bats and lizards, all built on a similar bone plan but adapted for different uses)

Analogous structures serve a similar function but have a different structural origin/design (e.g. the wings of birds and the wings of insects - both used for flight but structurally very different, with no common ancestral origin for the wing itself)
Homologous structures suggest that the organisms sharing them evolved from a common ancestor, since the shared underlying design is best explained by common descent, later modified for different uses

questions.model_answer: Homologous structures are organs that share the same basic structural design or evolutionary origin, even though they may now perform different functions in different organisms - for example, the forelimbs of humans, bats and lizards are all built on essentially the same underlying bone arrangement, despite being adapted respectively for grasping, flying and walking. Analogous structures, in contrast, serve a similar function but arose independently with different underlying structures - for example, the wings of birds and the wings of insects both enable flight, but are built completely differently and did not evolve from a shared winged ancestor. Homologous structures provide strong evidence for evolution because their shared underlying design, despite different present-day functions, is best explained by descent from a common ancestor whose original structure was later modified by natural selection for different purposes in different lineages.

notes.overview: This chapter studies ecosystems - how living organisms (biotic components) interact with each other and with non-living factors (abiotic components) like sunlight, water and soil - focusing on food chains and food webs, how energy flows through an ecosystem, the roles of producers/consumers/decomposers, and the environmental impact of waste, especially the difference between biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances.

sections.title: 1. Ecosystem - Biotic and Abiotic Components
sections.content: An ecosystem consists of all the living organisms (biotic components - plants, animals, microorganisms) in an area, interacting with each other and with the non-living (abiotic) components of their environment, such as sunlight, temperature, water, soil and air. Ecosystems can be natural (forest, pond) or artificial (garden, aquarium).

sections.title: 2. Food Chains and Trophic Levels
sections.content: A food chain is a sequence of organisms where each one feeds on the one before it, starting with a producer (green plants, which make their own food via photosynthesis). Each step is a trophic level: producers (1st), primary consumers/herbivores (2nd), secondary consumers/small carnivores (3rd), tertiary consumers/top carnivores (4th).
keywords: producer -> primary consumer -> secondary consumer -> tertiary consumer
trophic level = each step/link in the food chain

sections.title: 3. Food Webs
sections.content: In nature, food chains are rarely isolated - they interconnect into a food web, since most organisms eat (and are eaten by) more than one other type of organism. Food webs give an ecosystem more stability than a single linear food chain, since the loss of one species has more alternative paths for energy flow to continue through.
keywords: food webs add stability to an ecosystem
sections.video_title: Difference between Food Chain and Food Web (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 4. Flow of Energy - The 10% Law
sections.content: Only about 1% of the solar energy falling on green plants' leaves is actually captured and converted into chemical (food) energy through photosynthesis. Further, at each step of a food chain, only about 10% of the energy available at one trophic level is transferred to the next (the '10% law') - the rest is lost as heat through life processes like respiration. This is why food chains rarely extend beyond 3-4 trophic levels - there simply isn't enough energy left to support a 5th level.
keywords: only ~1% of sunlight captured by plants
10% law: ~10% of energy passes to the next trophic level
energy loss limits food chains to 3-4 levels
sections.video_title: Flow of Energy in Ecosystem (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 5. Decomposers
sections.content: Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down the complex organic compounds in dead plants and animals (and their waste) into simpler inorganic substances that go back into the soil, to be reused by plants. Decomposers act at every trophic level (breaking down producers, herbivores and carnivores alike), so they are not assigned a single fixed position within a food chain the way other organisms are.
keywords: decomposers break down organic matter into inorganic substances
act at every trophic level, not a single fixed position
sections.video_title: Components of Ecosystem Part 2 - Producers, Consumers, Decomposers (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 6. Ozone Layer and its Depletion
sections.content: The ozone layer, present in the upper atmosphere (stratosphere), absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun, protecting life on Earth. Its depletion, caused mainly by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) released from refrigerants, aerosols and some industrial processes, allows more UV radiation to reach the Earth's surface, increasing risks like skin cancer.
sections.video_title: Ozone Layer and How It is Getting Depleted (Magnet Brains)

sections.title: 7. Biodegradable and Non-Biodegradable Waste
sections.content: Biodegradable substances (like food waste, paper, cotton) are broken down by microorganisms into simpler, harmless substances over time. Non-biodegradable substances (like plastics, metals, glass) are not broken down by microorganisms and persist in the environment for a very long time, accumulating and causing pollution. Waste management strategies (the 5 R's: Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle) aim to minimise the environmental impact of both types of waste.
keywords: 5 R's: Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle

key_terms.Ecosystem: All living organisms in an area, interacting with each other and their non-living environment.
key_terms.Food chain: A sequence of organisms, each feeding on the one before it, starting with a producer.
key_terms.Food web: A network of interconnected food chains within an ecosystem.
key_terms.Trophic level: Each successive step/link in a food chain.
key_terms.Decomposer: An organism (bacteria/fungi) that breaks down dead organic matter into simpler inorganic substances.
key_terms.Biodegradable: A substance that can be broken down by microorganisms into harmless products.
key_terms.Non-biodegradable: A substance that resists breakdown by microorganisms and persists in the environment.

important_facts: Only about 1% of the solar energy incident on a plant's leaves is captured as chemical energy via photosynthesis.
At each trophic level, only about 10% of the energy is passed on to the next level (the 10% law); the rest is lost mostly as heat.
Food chains are usually limited to 3-4 trophic levels because of this progressive energy loss.
Decomposers act at every trophic level, breaking down organic matter into inorganic substances that return to the soil.
The ozone layer absorbs harmful UV radiation; CFCs are the main cause of its depletion.
Biodegradable waste is broken down by microorganisms; non-biodegradable waste is not and persists in the environment.
exam_tips: When asked why food chains rarely have more than 4 trophic levels, always cite the 10% law (energy loss at each step) rather than just saying 'not enough food'.
Remember decomposers are deliberately NOT given a fixed trophic level - if a question asks why, the answer is that they act at every level, not just one.

For waste management questions, be able to distinguish the 5 R's clearly: Refuse (don't accept unnecessary items), Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again as-is), Repurpose (use for a different function), Recycle (process into a new product).

questions.model_answer: At each step of a food chain, only about 10% of the energy available at one trophic level is transferred to the next; the remaining approximately 90% is lost mainly as heat through life processes like respiration. Because of this large energy loss at every step, by the time you reach the 4th or 5th trophic level, there is too little energy left to support a viable population - which is why food chains are generally limited to 3-4 trophic levels.

questions.question: The international agreement signed in 1987 to control the production of ozone-depleting substances is called the:
questions.explanation: The Montreal Protocol (1987) is the international treaty to phase out substances (like CFCs) responsible for ozone layer depletion.

questions.question: Which of the following is a biodegradable substance?
questions.explanation: Paper is made from natural cellulose fibres and can be broken down by microorganisms, making it biodegradable.

questions.question: The stability of an ecosystem is generally improved by:
options: having a simple, single food chain
having greater biodiversity and interconnected food webs
questions.explanation: Greater biodiversity and interconnected food webs give an ecosystem more alternative energy pathways, making it more resilient to disturbance.

questions.question: The increasing concentration of harmful chemicals (like pesticides) at successive trophic levels of a food chain is called:
questions.explanation: Biomagnification is the phenomenon where non-biodegradable chemicals accumulate in increasing concentration as they pass up the food chain, since they are not broken down or excreted easily.

questions.question: Excessive exposure to UV radiation (due to ozone depletion) is particularly known to cause which health problem in humans?
questions.explanation: The ozone layer absorbs most of the sun's harmful UV-B radiation; its depletion increases the risk of skin cancer and cataracts in humans.

questions.question: What is biomagnification? Why does it become a bigger problem for organisms at higher trophic levels?

rubric.point: Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of harmful, non-biodegradable chemicals as they move up the food chain
Organisms at higher trophic levels eat many organisms from the level below, so the chemicals accumulate more in their bodies

questions.model_answer: Biomagnification is the phenomenon where the concentration of harmful, non-biodegradable chemicals (such as pesticides) increases at each successive trophic level of a food chain. It is a bigger problem for organisms at higher trophic levels because they consume many organisms from the level below them, so these chemicals keep accumulating in their bodies, reaching the highest and most harmful concentration in top carnivores (including humans).

questions.question: Name two human activities/substances responsible for the depletion of the ozone layer, and state one effect of this depletion.

rubric.point: Name CFCs (from refrigerators, aerosols, air conditioners) as a main cause
State an effect, e.g. increased UV radiation reaching earth causing skin cancer/cataracts

questions.model_answer: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), released from refrigerators, air conditioners and aerosol sprays, are the main human-made substances responsible for ozone depletion. This depletion allows more harmful UV radiation to reach the Earth's surface, increasing the risk of skin cancer and cataracts in humans.

questions.question: Why are food webs considered more ecologically stable than simple, isolated food chains?

rubric.point: A food web has multiple interconnected feeding pathways
If one species is lost/declines, energy can still flow through alternative paths, so the ecosystem is less disrupted

questions.model_answer: A food web consists of many interconnected food chains, giving multiple feeding pathways between organisms. If one species is removed or declines, energy can still flow through alternative paths in the web, so the ecosystem is disrupted much less than it would be if it depended on a single, isolated food chain.

questions.question: Suggest two practices that can help manage non-biodegradable waste more responsibly.

rubric.point: Any valid practice such as reducing use of single-use plastics
Any second valid practice such as recycling, or segregating waste at source

questions.model_answer: Two useful practices are: (1) reducing the use of single-use plastics and switching to biodegradable/reusable alternatives, and (2) segregating waste at source into biodegradable and non-biodegradable categories so that non-biodegradable waste can be properly recycled rather than sent to landfills.

questions.question: What is a trophic level? Identify the trophic level of a secondary consumer.

rubric.point: A trophic level is each step or stage in a food chain, representing a feeding position
A secondary consumer occupies the third trophic level

questions.model_answer: A trophic level is each successive step or stage in a food chain, occupied by an organism based on its feeding position (e.g. producer, primary consumer). A secondary consumer, which eats primary consumers (herbivores), occupies the third trophic level.

questions.question: Explain what biomagnification is, using a suitable example of a food chain to illustrate how it happens.

rubric.point: Define biomagnification as increasing concentration of harmful chemicals up the food chain
Give a valid example food chain (e.g. water with pesticide -> algae -> small fish -> large fish -> bird)
Explain that each predator accumulates the chemical from all its prey, so the top consumer has the highest concentration

questions.model_answer: Biomagnification is the progressive increase in the concentration of harmful, non-biodegradable chemicals (such as pesticides) as they pass through successive trophic levels of a food chain. For example, in a water body contaminated with a pesticide: algae absorb small amounts, small fish that eat large quantities of algae accumulate more, larger fish that eat many small fish accumulate even more, and a fish-eating bird at the top of the chain ends up with the highest concentration - since each predator consumes many organisms from the level below, concentrating the chemical each step.

questions.question: How is ozone formed in the upper atmosphere, and why is the ozone layer important for life on Earth?

rubric.point: Ozone (O3) is formed when UV radiation splits O2 molecules into free oxygen atoms, which combine with other O2 molecules
The ozone layer sits in the upper atmosphere (stratosphere)
It absorbs most harmful UV-B radiation from the sun, protecting living organisms from its damaging effects

questions.model_answer: In the upper atmosphere (stratosphere), high-energy UV radiation from the sun splits some oxygen (O2) molecules into individual oxygen atoms. These atoms combine with other O2 molecules to form ozone (O3). The ozone layer is important because it absorbs most of the sun's harmful UV-B radiation before it reaches the Earth's surface, protecting living organisms from radiation damage that can cause skin cancer, cataracts, and harm to crops and marine life.

questions.topic: Comparing food chain and food web
questions.question: Differentiate between a food chain and a food web. Which one is more commonly found in nature, and why?

rubric.point: Food chain = single linear sequence of feeding relationships
Food web = interconnected network of multiple overlapping food chains
Food webs are more common in nature since most organisms eat/are eaten by more than one species

questions.model_answer: A food chain is a single, linear sequence in which each organism feeds on the one before it (e.g. grass -> deer -> tiger). A food web is a more complex, interconnected network formed by many overlapping food chains. Food webs are more commonly found in nature because most organisms do not rely on just one food source or have just one predator - they eat, and are eaten by, multiple different species, creating many interlinked pathways.

questions.question: List three harmful effects of ozone layer depletion on living organisms and the environment.

rubric.point: Effect 1: increased skin cancer/cataracts in humans due to more UV-B reaching earth
Effect 2: damage to crops and reduced plant growth/yield
Effect 3: harm to aquatic life, especially phytoplankton, disrupting marine food chains

questions.model_answer: Three harmful effects of ozone depletion are: (1) increased incidence of skin cancer and cataracts in humans, since more UV-B radiation reaches the Earth's surface; (2) damage to crops and reduced plant growth/yield, harming agriculture; (3) harm to aquatic ecosystems, particularly to phytoplankton near the ocean surface, which disrupts marine food chains that depend on them as producers.

questions.question: Explain why non-biodegradable waste is a bigger environmental concern than biodegradable waste, and suggest two ways to manage it.

rubric.point: Non-biodegradable waste is not broken down by decomposers and persists in the environment for a very long time
It can accumulate in soil/water and enter food chains, causing biomagnification
Two valid management suggestions, e.g. recycling and reducing use/switching to biodegradable alternatives

questions.model_answer: Non-biodegradable waste (plastics, DDT, metals) cannot be broken down by decomposers, so it persists in the environment for a very long time, accumulating in soil and water bodies. It can also enter food chains and cause biomagnification, harming organisms at higher trophic levels. It can be managed by: (1) recycling non-biodegradable materials wherever possible instead of discarding them, and (2) reducing their use, for example by replacing single-use plastics with biodegradable or reusable alternatives.

questions.topic: Comprehensive - energy flow and the 10% law
questions.question: (a) State the 10% law of energy flow in an ecosystem. (b) If a producer captures 100,000 J of solar energy, calculate the energy available to a tertiary consumer (4th trophic level), showing your working. (c) Explain why food chains rarely have more than 4-5 trophic levels.

rubric.point: (a) State the 10% law: only about 10% of energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next
(b) Correctly calculate energy at each level: producer 100000 -> primary consumer 10000 -> secondary consumer 1000 -> tertiary consumer 100 J
(c) Explain that repeated 90% energy loss at each step leaves too little energy to support further trophic levels

questions.model_answer: (a) The 10% law states that only about 10% of the energy available at one trophic level is transferred to the next trophic level; the remaining 90% is lost mainly as heat through life processes like respiration. (b) Producer: 100,000 J. Primary consumer (10%): 10,000 J. Secondary consumer (10% of that): 1,000 J. Tertiary consumer (10% of that): 100 J. So the tertiary consumer has 100 J available. (c) Since roughly 90% of energy is lost at each trophic level, the amount of usable energy drops very rapidly. By the 4th or 5th level, so little energy remains that it cannot support a viable population at yet another level, which is why food chains are generally limited to 3-4 trophic levels.

questions.topic: Comprehensive - ozone layer, depletion and protection
questions.question: (a) What is the ozone layer and where is it located? (b) Name the main substances responsible for its depletion and their common sources. (c) Describe two effects of ozone depletion. (d) What international step has been taken to address this problem?

rubric.point: (a) Ozone layer is a layer of O3 in the stratosphere (upper atmosphere)
(b) Name CFCs, with sources like refrigerants, aerosol sprays, air conditioners
(c) Describe two valid effects, e.g. skin cancer/cataracts and crop/marine life damage
(d) Mention the Montreal Protocol (1987) as the international agreement to phase out ozone-depleting substances

questions.model_answer: (a) The ozone layer is a region of the stratosphere (upper atmosphere) containing a relatively high concentration of ozone (O3) gas, which shields the Earth from harmful solar UV radiation. (b) Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are the main substances responsible for ozone depletion; they are released from refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol sprays, and some industrial processes. (c) Two effects: increased UV-B radiation reaching Earth raises the risk of skin cancer and cataracts in humans, and it damages crops and harms aquatic organisms like phytoplankton, disrupting marine food chains. (d) The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, is the key international agreement under which countries committed to phasing out the production and use of ozone-depleting substances like CFCs.

questions.topic: Energy flow to the next trophic level
questions.question: Plants receive energy from the Sun and use it for several processes: growth, photosynthesis, respiration, and transport of substances. Energy used for which of these processes gets transferred to the next trophic level (the consumers that eat the plant)?
options: Only transport of substances and reproduction
All of growth, photosynthesis, respiration and transport
questions.explanation: Only the energy that goes into building the plant's own body mass (growth) is stored in a form that a consumer eating the plant can obtain; energy used for respiration, transport etc. is dissipated as heat/used up in life processes and is not passed on to the next trophic level.

questions.topic: Trophic level position and energy received
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Omnivores receive 10% of their energy from the trophic level below them.
Reason (R): An omnivore is always in the trophic level just above herbivores.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: A is true - by the 10% law, any consumer receives only about 10% of the energy stored in the trophic level it feeds from. R is false: omnivores eat both plants and animals from multiple trophic levels, not exclusively from the level just above herbivores.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): All kitchen waste cannot be turned into compost.
Reason (R): Material like milk packets may not be biodegradable.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both are true, and R correctly explains A: some kitchen waste includes non-biodegradable material (like plastic milk packets), which cannot be broken down by decomposers and therefore cannot become compost.

questions.topic: Inverted pyramid of energy in aquatic ecosystems
questions.question: In a traditional land-ecosystem food pyramid, producers outweigh primary consumers, and so on up the pyramid. In some aquatic ecosystems, an inverted pyramid of biomass exists instead: the total mass of producers (phytoplankton) is much smaller than the mass of the top consumers (large fish). (a) Even so, which trophic level is likely to have the greatest amount of energy captured in such an aquatic ecosystem? Give a reason. (b) Such aquatic ecosystems are not considered sustainable - justify this statement.

rubric.point: The producers (phytoplankton) still have the greatest amount of energy captured from sunlight, since energy captured (not standing biomass) always decreases as you move up trophic levels, following the 10% law

Because the standing mass at the lower (producer) trophic level is so small, there is limited food available to support the higher trophic levels over time, so the ecosystem cannot sustain itself long-term without organisms starving/dying off sooner than in a normal pyramid

questions.model_answer: Even in an inverted-biomass aquatic ecosystem, the producers (phytoplankton) still capture the greatest total amount of energy from sunlight, since the energy actually available at each trophic level always decreases going up the food chain (by the 10% law) - only the standing biomass, not the flow of energy, is inverted here. Such ecosystems are considered less sustainable because the small standing mass of producers can only support a limited, constantly turning-over supply of food; since there isn't a large standing stock of food at the base, the higher trophic levels depend on the continuous, rapid reproduction of phytoplankton rather than an accumulated reserve, making the system more fragile and prone to organisms dying off sooner if that turnover is disrupted.

questions.topic: Ozone layer depletion - cause and health effect
questions.question: A marked decline in the thickness of the ozone layer was noticed in the 1980s. (a) Which human activity is chiefly responsible for this? (b) What is a possible effect of ozone depletion on human health?

rubric.point: Release of CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons), used in refrigerants, aerosol sprays etc., is the chief human activity responsible for ozone layer depletion
A thinner ozone layer lets more harmful UV radiation reach the Earth's surface, which is known to cause skin cancer (and other harms like cataracts) in humans

questions.model_answer: The release of chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) - used in refrigerants, air conditioners and aerosol sprays - is the human activity chiefly responsible for depleting the ozone layer. Since the ozone layer normally absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation, a thinner ozone layer allows more UV radiation to reach the Earth's surface, which is known to cause skin cancer (and other harms, such as cataracts) in humans.

questions.topic: Unidirectional flow of energy in a food chain
questions.question: Explain, with reasoning, why the flow of energy in a food chain is said to be unidirectional.

rubric.point: Energy captured by autotrophs (producers) from sunlight flows only forward, to herbivores and then carnivores, at each successive trophic level
This energy does not flow back - the energy captured by producers never reverts to the solar input, and the energy passed to herbivores never returns to the producers

As energy moves progressively through the trophic levels, it becomes unavailable to the earlier/previous trophic levels, and is also progressively lost as heat at each step - so the flow only ever proceeds forward, never backward

questions.model_answer: The flow of energy through a food chain is unidirectional because it only ever moves forward, never backward, between trophic levels. Autotrophs (producers) capture energy from sunlight and convert it into chemical energy in their bodies; this energy then passes to herbivores that eat the producers, and on to carnivores that eat the herbivores, and so on - but at no point does any of this energy revert back to an earlier stage. The energy captured by producers doesn't go back into the sunlight it came from, and the energy that passes into herbivores doesn't return to the producers. Moreover, a large fraction of energy is lost as heat (through respiration and other life processes) at every single transfer, so once energy has moved on to the next trophic level, it becomes permanently unavailable to the trophic levels before it - this one-way, ever-diminishing transfer is what makes the flow of energy in a food chain unidirectional.

questions.topic: Impact of losing a trophic level and biomagnification
questions.question: (a) If all the organisms of one trophic level in a food chain were to die out, what impact would this have on the population of organisms in the trophic level below it? Explain. (b) Name the phenomenon in which non-degradable chemicals progressively accumulate at each trophic level, reaching their highest concentration in the bodies of top consumers.

rubric.point: If a trophic level's organisms die out, the population at the trophic level immediately below it is likely to increase, since it is no longer being consumed/kept in check by the level above
This phenomenon (of non-degradable chemicals accumulating progressively up the food chain) is called biomagnification

questions.model_answer: If all the organisms of one trophic level die out, the population of the trophic level immediately below it is likely to increase, since those organisms are no longer being consumed/preyed upon by the level that has disappeared, removing that predation pressure. The phenomenon in which non-biodegradable chemicals progressively accumulate in concentration at each successive trophic level, reaching their highest levels in the bodies of top consumers, is called biomagnification.

questions.question: If all the organisms of one trophic level in a food chain die, what would be the impact on the population of organisms in the trophic level immediately below it?

It will increase in the next trophic level
It will increase in the lower trophic level
It will remain the same in the lower trophic level
questions.explanation: With the consuming trophic level gone, organisms at the level immediately below are no longer preyed upon, so their population tends to increase.

questions.topic: Why aquariums need cleaning but natural ponds don't
questions.question:
Assertion (A): A natural pond does not need to be artificially cleaned, but an aquarium does.
Reason (R): A natural pond is a complete, self-sustaining ecosystem with decomposers that recycle waste, whereas an aquarium is an artificial, incomplete ecosystem that lacks this natural self-cleaning balance.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R explains A: a natural pond contains a full community of producers, consumers and decomposers that together recycle nutrients and break down waste, keeping the ecosystem self-sustaining; an aquarium, being a small artificial and incomplete ecosystem, lacks this natural balance (particularly a sufficient decomposer community), so waste and excess nutrients build up unless removed manually.

questions.topic: Only a small fraction of sunlight is used in photosynthesis
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Only about 1% of the solar radiation falling on green plants is actually absorbed and used for photosynthesis.
Reason (R): Most of the sunlight falling on a plant is either reflected away, transmitted through the leaves, or absorbed and lost as heat, rather than being captured by chlorophyll for photosynthesis.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
questions.explanation: Both statements are true, and R explains A: only a small fraction of incident sunlight is actually of the right wavelengths, correctly oriented and absorbed by chlorophyll to drive photosynthesis - most sunlight is reflected, passes through the leaf, or is dissipated as heat, explaining why the overall efficiency of solar energy capture by plants is so low (roughly 1%).

questions.topic: Numerical - working backward through the 10% law of energy transfer
questions.question: In the food chain Grass -> Grasshopper -> Frog -> Snake -> Hawk, if the amount of energy available at the fourth trophic level (the snake) is 5 kJ, how much energy was originally available at the producer (grass) level? (Assume the standard 10% law of energy transfer between trophic levels.)

rubric.point: The snake is the 4th trophic level; grass (the producer) is the 1st trophic level, so there are 3 transfer steps between them (1st->2nd->3rd->4th), each retaining only 10% of the previous level's energy
Working backward, each step up the chain multiplies energy by 10 (since only 10% survives moving forward): 5 kJ x 10 x 10 x 10 = 5000 kJ

questions.model_answer: Grass (the producer) is the 1st trophic level, and the snake is the 4th, so there are three energy-transfer steps between them (grass to grasshopper, grasshopper to frog, frog to snake), each of which retains only about 10% of the energy of the previous level, by the 10% law. Working backward from the snake's 5 kJ, each step back up the chain requires multiplying by 10 (since only a tenth of the energy survives moving forward): 5 kJ x 10 x 10 x 10 = 5000 kJ. So approximately 5000 kJ of energy was originally available at the producer (grass) level.
